card.title: Hybridization Involving s and p Orbitals

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Hybridisation is the orbital answer to VSEPR's shape count: same-shell s and p orbitals blend into equivalent, strongly directed hybrids — four sp³ pointing to a tetrahedron (CH₄ at 109.5°), three sp² in a plane (C₂H₄, BF₃ at 120°, one p orbital left over for π), two sp in a line (C₂H₂, BeCl₂ at 180°, two p orbitals for two π bonds).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - sp³: 4 hybrids, 109.5°; sp²: 3 hybrids + 1p, 120°; sp: 2 hybrids + 2p, 180° - s-character: sp 50% > sp² 33% > sp³ 25% - Bond strength/shortness ∝ s-character

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **sp³ ≠ four bonds always:** NH₃ (3 bonds) and H₂O (2 bonds) are sp³ — the hybrid count is four; bonds are what remain after lone pairs occupy hybrids.  ·  **Promotion is an investment, not a loss:** the promotion energy is repaid by the extra bond energies of four strong sp³ bonds versus two weak pure-p bonds.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Specialized insight for 08 hybridization involving s and p orbitals only.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Methane's four identical bonds*** — impossible for raw 2s/2p orbitals (one s bond would differ from three p bonds); sp³ mixing makes all four equivalent, as NMR and bond lengths confirm.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Hybridisation and VSEPR agree by construction: the domain count from VSEPR equals the hybrid count from VBT — use VSEPR for shape, hybridisation for the orbital explanation behind it.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Hybridisation: same-shell s+p orbitals mix → equivalent directed hybrids; number conserved; large lobes overlap better. sp³ (4, tetrahedral 109.5°): CH₄, NH₃, H₂O. sp² (3, trigonal planar 120° + 1 p ⟂): C₂H₄, BF₃, SO₂. sp (2, linear 180° + 2 p ⟂): C₂H₂, BeCl₂, CO₂. s-character ladder sp > sp² > sp³ in bond strength.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Ethyne's sp C–H bonds (50% s-character) are acidic enough (pKₐ ≈ 25) to form acetylides with strong bases — hybridisation strength you can deprotonate.

rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Mixing Orbitals to Point Bonds Carbon's ground-state configuration (1s² 2s² 2p²) promises two bonds; methane delivers four identical ones at 109.5°. The rescue is **hybridisation**: before bonding, the central atom's s and p orbitals of the same shell blend into new **equivalent hybrid orbitals**, whose shapes and directions are tailor-made for…  ·  ## 2. Comparison Tables **The three hybridisations at a glance** | Property | sp | sp² | sp³ | |---|---|---|---| | Orbitals mixed | 1s + 1p | 1s + 2p | 1s + 3p | | Hybrids formed | 2 | 3 | 4 | | Geometry | Linear | Trigonal planar | Tetrahedral | | Angle | 180° | 120° | 109.5° | | s-character | 50% | 33% | 25% | |…  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **Hybridisation is per-bonding-event, not a free-atom property:** an isolated carbon does not "contain" sp³ orbitals; they exist in the molecule, formed as bonds form.  ·  **Lone pairs occupy hybrids too:** NH₃ and H₂O are sp³ — the lone pairs sit in sp³ hybrids; that is why their angles are near-tetrahedral rather than 90°.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **More p-character ≠ stronger bond:** s-character strengthens (closer to nucleus) — sp bonds beat sp³ bonds in strength and shortness.  ·  ## 7.
